opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest source of disorder is that the industry hasn't agreed on what problem it's actually solving. Everyone says "embodied intelligence," but people mean very different things by it.

Some companies are really hardware companies. They build beautiful humanoid bodies that can do backflips or dance at a gala, and the demos look amazing. But a backflip is mostly a control problem. It's pre-planned motion, and it doesn't show the robot can understand an unfamiliar environment, pick up an object it's never seen, or finish a useful task reliably. Other companies are essentially model companies. They talk about foundation models and VLAs, but their robots never leave the lab and never face a real customer. Then there's a third group chasing whatever the capital market wants that quarter. When investors want humanoids, everyone ships legs. When they want "general-purpose brains," everyone pivots their pitch deck.

So you get a lot of noise: demos optimized for video rather than deployment, teleoperated clips presented as if they were autonomous, and valuations driven by narrative rather than by the robot working eight hours a day in a pharmacy or a factory.

Underneath all that, I think the root cause is data. Language models had the internet. We don't have an internet of robot actions. Collecting real-world teleoperation data is expensive and slow, and it doesn't scale the way people hope. Everyone is quietly struggling with this, and because nobody has fully solved it, there's room for many contradictory stories at once. My own view is that large-scale synthetic data and simulation, combined with a smaller amount of real data, is the path that can actually scale. Not everyone agrees, and that disagreement is part of the disorder too.

The healthy correction will come from commercialization. Once robots have to earn their keep in real scenarios, closing the loop on a task with high success rates, a lot of this confusion gets filtered out very quickly. Reality is a very good judge.

r001.rationale: It contrasts demos and investor narratives with robots reliably completing useful work in real deployments.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute the disorder to greater U.S. tolerance for innovation.

r003.rationale: It does not identify any U.S. companies or group as the industry's biggest bubble.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest source of disorder is that people haven't agreed on what the real problem is, so everyone is optimizing for different things and calling it the same thing.

Some teams are fundamentally hardware companies. They build a very impressive humanoid, it walks, it dances, it does a backflip in a demo video, and investors get excited. But locomotion and manipulation are completely different problems. Walking is largely a control problem, and we've known how to make it work for a while. Making a hand pick up a cup it has never seen before, in a kitchen it has never been in, and not knock over the plate next to it, that's a generalization problem, and that's where the actual intelligence lives. A lot of the noise comes from conflating the two.

Then there's the data question, which is where I see the most confusion. Some people say just collect massive amounts of teleoperation data and scale like a language model. Some say the answer is simulation. Some say internet video. Each camp speaks as if the others are obviously wrong, but honestly none of us have the kind of evidence that would settle it yet. Real-robot data is expensive and slow, simulation has the sim-to-real gap, and video doesn't give you actions. My own view is that you need synthetic data as the backbone to get coverage and diversity, and real data to anchor it, but I'd be lying if I said that debate was closed.

The third thing is the mismatch between timelines and capital. There's a lot of money that came in expecting a ChatGPT moment for robots within a couple of years. That pressure pushes companies to show something, anything, that looks like progress, so you get polished demos that don't reflect robustness. When you watch a demo, the question to ask is not "can it do this," it's "what's the success rate across a hundred trials, in a scene it wasn't tuned for." Very few companies will tell you that number.

So I'd summarize it as: unclear problem definition, no consensus on the data recipe, and capital on a shorter clock than the science. Those three feed each other. I actually think it's a healthy kind of chaos in the sense that the field is early and exploring, but it does mean a lot of companies will find out in a year or two that they were solving the wrong problem well.

r001.rationale: The response points to unclear problem definitions, disagreement about data, and mismatched capital timelines. It does not identify a divide between delivering real productivity and merely telling stories.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute industry disorder to greater U.S. tolerance for innovation.

r003.rationale: It does not identify U.S. embodied-intelligence companies as the industry's biggest bubble.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest source of disorder is that companies are pursuing very different things under the same label. Some are building robot hardware, some are developing models, and some are trying to deliver a complete solution for a particular task. Yet they’re often compared as if they were solving the same problem.

That makes it easy for a compelling demonstration to stand in for real progress. A robot completing a task once is very different from completing it reliably, in unfamiliar conditions, at a cost a customer can accept. Until we’re clearer about the task, the operating conditions, and the standard of success, companies will keep chasing different targets while claiming to lead the same race.

r001.rationale: It contrasts compelling demonstrations with reliable task completion in unfamiliar conditions at a customer-acceptable cost, conveying the gap between claimed progress and practical productivity.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute the disorder to greater U.S. tolerance for innovation.

r003.rationale: It does not identify U.S. embodied-intelligence companies as the industry's biggest bubble.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest source of disorder is that the industry hasn’t agreed on what problem it’s trying to solve. Some companies are building robot bodies, some are developing models, and some are delivering complete systems for specific applications, but they’re often judged as if they’re doing the same thing.

That makes it easy to confuse a compelling demonstration with a viable product. A robot completing a task once is very different from completing it reliably, at an acceptable cost, in a customer’s environment. Until those practical requirements become the basis for comparison, companies will keep chasing different targets while telling very similar stories.

r001.rationale: It contrasts one-off demonstrations and similar stories with reliable, affordable products, but does not clearly identify the central divide as real productivity versus merely telling stories.
